entries.purpose: Protect a stored member or administrator password against an attacker who reads the database

strength.basis: The encoder writes a 32-byte Argon2id output over a 16-byte salt, and Bouncy Castle computes it. What makes guessing expensive is the cost above rather than the output length.

entries.storageBoundary: The instance database, in user_account.password_hash. The salt and the parameters travel inside the encoding; there is no separate key.
entries.permittedUse: Encoding a replacement password, verifying a sign-in or recent full-authentication proof, re-encoding a stored hash that sits below the current parameters, and the start-up warm-up, which encodes and verifies a fixed password of its own in memory and never reads an account. Never for a digest, an identifier or a signature.
entries.rotation: Raising the memory cost or the iteration count is the rotation, and a stored hash below either is re-encoded on its owner's next successful sign-in; storing that is best effort, so a database failure leaves the old hash in place rather than failing the login. Spring Security compares only those two, so changing the parallelism, the salt length or the hash length alone does not re-encode anything already stored, and existing hashes keep the parameters they were written with until one of the other two moves.
entries.revocation: Issuing a new credential or choosing a new permanent password replaces the hash and ends every session of the account.
entries.recovery: None is possible or needed: a hash is not recoverable by design, and a member who cannot sign in is given a new credential.
entries.retirement: Argon2id is replaced by encoding new and re-encoded passwords under the successor while the old encoding stays verifiable, which is what the re-encode path already does for a parameter change.

entries.purpose: The one-time password an instance mails a member for their first sign-in

strength.basis: Twenty-four bytes drawn from SecureRandom, so the credential a member is mailed is exactly as hard to guess as the bytes behind it.

entries.storageBoundary: Generated in memory, mailed to the member, and kept only as its Argon2id hash. The plaintext is never written to the database, a log or an administrative screen.
entries.permittedUse: One sign-in, after which the account must set a permanent password. It cannot become that permanent password.
entries.rotation: Issuing a credential again replaces the previous one and ends every session of the account.
entries.revocation: Withdrawing an unused credential clears the hash and its deadline.
entries.recovery: None: a lost credential is reissued, never recovered.
entries.retirement: Retired with the account, whose deactivation ends its sessions.

entries.purpose: The single-use code an instance mails a member who asked to set a new password themselves

strength.basis: Eight characters drawn from a thirty-symbol alphabet, which is what a member can retype from a mail without having to choose between two glyphs that look alike. Thirty-nine bits is far below what a secret standing on its own would need, and it does not stand on its own: what bounds guessing is the budget an attacker gets, not the size of the value. Every attempt spends the credential-verification limit on the caller's own address and a permit in the verification pool, the code lives for a club setting of at most a day, and redeeming one deletes it.

entries.storageBoundary: Generated in memory, mailed to the member, and kept only as its SHA-256 in the outstanding-code row. The plaintext is never written to the database, a log or an administrative screen. docs/security-risks.md records what that digest is worth to somebody who reads the database, and why it is not a keyed one.
entries.permittedUse: One redemption, which sets the password the member typed and ends every session of the account. It never becomes the password, and it authorises nothing else.
entries.rotation: Asking for a code again replaces the outstanding one, and the code that was replaced stops working at that moment.
entries.revocation: Redemption, expiry and the retention sweep each delete the row. Anything that moves the account's security epoch or its address leaves the row in place and makes it unredeemable, because redemption compares both against the account as it is then; the sweep removes it once its deadline passes. After any of them the code reads as one nobody holds.
entries.recovery: None: a code a member no longer has is asked for again, never recovered.
entries.retirement: Retired with the account, whose deactivation withdraws any code still outstanding.

entries.purpose: Tell whether the address a reset code went to is still the address the account holds, without the outstanding-code table keeping an address

strength.basis: The collision resistance of SHA-256's 256-bit output. The digest keeps an address out of the table that holds outstanding codes; it is not offered as protection against somebody who already knows the address.

entries.storageBoundary: The instance database, as the address fingerprint on the outstanding-code row. It is written when a code is mailed and removed with the row.
entries.permittedUse: Comparing the address a code was mailed to against the one the account holds at redemption, so that correcting an address withdraws the code that went to the old one. It is not an authenticator and it names nobody on its own.
entries.rotation: Not applicable: no key exists. A row is replaced when a new code is asked for.
entries.revocation: Not applicable.
entries.recovery: None is needed: the row is deleted rather than repaired.
entries.retirement: A successor digest changes what the stored fingerprints mean, so outstanding rows are cleared with the change rather than migrated. Nothing outside the redemption path reads them.

entries.purpose: The numeric code a booking's players type at a keypad, installed per booking in an access-control system

strength.basis: The board sets the club's access code length to four to eight digits, so a code holds 13 to 26 bits. What bounds guessing is the keypad's own lockout and a validity window of a few hours, not the code's length; the same length governs the static codes a board types in.

entries.storageBoundary: Drawn into access_code, stored in clear so the access-control system and the players can be given it, and sent to that system. It never enters domain_event, a log, a problem body or the administrative API.
entries.permittedUse: Opening the access points of one booking during its validity window. The primary key on access_code keeps a code that a door may still accept from being drawn for a second grant.
entries.rotation: A code the access-control system rejects before its first acceptance is held until its exposure ends and replaced by a new draw. A move keeps the code.
entries.revocation: Revoking the grant removes it from the access-control system; the code stays held until the latest window any install asked for has ended, even after the removal is confirmed.
entries.recovery: None: a code is kept only while a door may accept it.
entries.retirement: The access pass deletes the detached row once its hold has ended.

entries.purpose: Verify an enrolled second factor with a time-based one-time code

strength.basis: Six decimal digits carry fewer than twenty bits. Password proof, account and address attempt budgets, the three-step acceptance window and a persisted last-consumed counter bound online guessing and replay. The shared secret contains 160 random bits.

entries.storageBoundary: The authenticator keeps the shared secret. Courtside reveals it only during setup and stores active and pending secrets encrypted under the separate instance keyring in account_mfa. Verification decrypts the secret in application memory.
entries.permittedUse: RFC 6238 second-factor proof after password authentication, including enrollment confirmation and sensitive-action reauthentication. HMAC-SHA-1 implements this protocol and is not used as a general digest or signature.
entries.rotation: Start a replacement enrollment and confirm a valid code before replacing the current secret. A pending setup expires after five minutes.
entries.revocation: Removing TOTP, disabling MFA or completing controlled account recovery removes the secret and revokes account sessions. The consumed step cannot authenticate again.
entries.recovery: Use another enrolled method or an unused recovery code. If every method is lost, controlled account recovery requires an identity check and a new permanent password.
entries.retirement: A protocol change requires a newly confirmed authenticator enrollment before the prior secret is removed.

entries.purpose: Encrypt account-bound TOTP secrets separately from the database and validate matching instance key material

parameters.associatedData: courtside-mfa prefix and immutable account UUID

strength.basis: SecureRandom supplies 256-bit encryption keys and independent 96-bit nonces. GCM uses a 128-bit authentication tag and binds each ciphertext to its account UUID. The tag bounds integrity strength.

entries.storageBoundary: Private mode-0600 keyrings live outside PostgreSQL in the persistent MFA key directory or an operator-selected file. PostgreSQL stores key identifiers, nonce and ciphertext envelopes plus an encrypted installation canary. Decrypted secrets remain in application memory.
entries.permittedUse: Encrypting and decrypting TOTP secrets and the installation canary. File locking serializes key publication and rotation. Constant-time MessageDigest comparison validates the decrypted canary, not a stored password or a content digest.
entries.rotation: The maintenance rotation atomically publishes a new random active key and retains every earlier key so existing ciphertext and backups remain decryptable.
entries.revocation: Removing a factor deletes its active and pending ciphertext. Rotation does not revoke old keys. Retiring a compromised key requires replacing affected enrollments and preserving or retiring backups that still require it.
entries.recovery: Complete backup and restore preserve database and matching keyrings together. Startup refuses missing or mismatched keys when encrypted enrollment data exists. A database-only dump requires the matching key material separately.
entries.retirement: Retain a key while any live ciphertext or retained backup requires it. Move to a successor encryption format only with a defined migration and matching restore support.

entries.purpose: Replace one second-factor proof or authorize controlled recovery after an external identity check

strength.basis: Twenty-four independent characters from a thirty-symbol alphabet provide more than 117 bits of entropy. Account and address budgets constrain redemption. A second-factor code also requires password proof; a controlled-recovery code expires under the configured reset-code lifetime.

entries.storageBoundary: The holder sees a second-factor recovery set only when generated. A controlled-recovery code travels through the registered email channel. The database stores domain-separated SHA-256 verifiers, never plaintext codes.
entries.permittedUse: One second-factor proof for an MFA-enabled account or one controlled account recovery with a new permanent password. Distinct verifier prefixes separate these purposes from ordinary password reset.
entries.rotation: Regenerating the recovery set invalidates its predecessor. Mailing a controlled-recovery code replaces the outstanding code for that rescue request.
entries.revocation: Atomic redemption consumes a second-factor code once. MFA disablement or completed controlled recovery clears the set. Controlled recovery also checks request identity, address, security epoch and expiry.
entries.recovery: Lost second-factor codes cannot be recovered. Use another enrolled method or request controlled recovery after an external identity check. The server-access maintenance path supports a locked-out sole administrator.
entries.retirement: A successor verifier format must invalidate or explicitly migrate outstanding codes before accepting the new format.

entries.purpose: Verify a domain-bound authenticator as an optional second factor after password proof

strength.basis: Spring Security supplies the advertised COSE algorithm set and WebAuthn4J verifies the selected signature. Courtside requires local user verification and binds each ceremony to its trusted origin, relying-party ID, account, session, purpose, security epoch and expiring challenge.

entries.storageBoundary: The authenticator retains the private key. PostgreSQL stores the credential public key, credential ID, user handle, signature counter, backup flags, original attestation and holder-private label. Courtside receives no biometric data and requests no manufacturer attestation.
entries.permittedUse: Registration and second-factor authentication with mandatory local user verification. Passwordless authentication and arbitrary request-host relying-party configuration are not supported.
entries.rotation: Enroll another named credential with recent full authentication proof, then remove the old credential. Each ceremony uses a new server-generated challenge.
entries.revocation: Individual removal, MFA disablement and completed controlled recovery delete credentials and revoke sessions. A consumed challenge cannot authenticate again, and nonzero signature counters must advance.
entries.recovery: Use another enrolled method or an unused recovery code. After a domain change, enroll a new credential on the new domain. Controlled recovery is required when every remaining method is lost.
entries.retirement: Changing the supported algorithm set must preserve verification of enrolled credentials or require replacement enrollment before their algorithm is removed.

entries.purpose: Compute TOTP proofs for synthetic browser and security-acceptance accounts

strength.basis: The fixtures compute the same six-digit protocol proof as an authenticator. Each uses its synthetic account setup secret and the selected acceptance clock. Application password proof and MFA attempt budgets remain in force.

entries.storageBoundary: The acceptance process keeps the synthetic setup secret and computed proof in memory. It supplies the proof only to that disposable account enrollment or login.
entries.permittedUse: Exercising actual TOTP enrollment, replay refusal and login against disposable acceptance deployments. It is never an operator credential or a production authenticator.
entries.rotation: Every browser journey starts from its own disposable account data and newly generated setup secret.
entries.revocation: The application consumes the TOTP step and removes the synthetic account with the acceptance dataset.
entries.recovery: Rerun the journey against a fresh acceptance dataset; no fixture secret needs to be recovered.
entries.retirement: Remove this helper with the TOTP browser journey or update it when the supported protocol changes.

entries.purpose: Create synthetic WebAuthn registration data and sign and independently verify assertions for the security acceptance harness

strength.basis: The fixture generates a P-256 key pair and signs the authenticator data plus the SHA-256 client-data digest with ECDSA-SHA256. The source key-generation gate rates this curve at 128 bits.

entries.storageBoundary: Each synthetic authenticator keeps its private key in the fixture process closure. Only the public key, credential identifier, signed data and attestation representation leave that process. The test independently checks signatures and COSE public-key coordinates.
entries.permittedUse: Producing and checking actual UV-marked WebAuthn protocol messages for disposable acceptance accounts. The fixture binds its configured HTTPS origin, RP ID, challenge, credential and increasing signature counter. It is not a hardware authenticator or a production credential provider.
entries.rotation: Each fixture authenticator generates a fresh key pair and random credential identifier.
entries.revocation: Removing the disposable account credential and terminating the fixture process retires its key. The application still enforces challenge consumption and account-session revocation.
entries.recovery: Rerun with a fresh synthetic authenticator. No private fixture key is retained for recovery.
entries.retirement: Replace the fixture protocol or algorithm together with its signature, COSE and live acceptance tests.

entries.purpose: Give an account with no credential a hash that no input can match, so an absent password is not an empty one

strength.basis: Thirty-two bytes drawn from SecureRandom, encoded, hashed and then dropped. Nothing keeps the plaintext, so no input matches the stored hash.

entries.storageBoundary: In memory only. The component is a singleton, so one value exists per process and it is discarded after encoding; nothing ever needs to reproduce it.
entries.permittedUse: Standing in for a credential that does not exist. It is never sent, shown, or successfully verified against a member's input.
entries.rotation: Every process start generates a new one. Nothing depends on the value, so there is no schedule to keep.
entries.revocation: Not applicable.
entries.recovery: None is possible, which is the point.
entries.retirement: Replaced with the password-hashing entry it shares an algorithm with.

entries.purpose: Give a stored row an identifier that names it without describing anybody

strength.basis: The 122 random bits a version-4 UUID draws. An identifier only has to be unique and no authorisation rests on one being hard to guess, so the 128-bit minimum does not reach it.

entries.storageBoundary: The instance database, as the primary key of the row it names, and the public API, which addresses rows by it.
entries.permittedUse: Naming a row. An identifier authenticates nothing and is not a capability: every endpoint that takes one still authorises the caller.
entries.rotation: Not applicable: an identifier that changed would no longer name the same row.
entries.revocation: Not applicable.
entries.recovery: None is needed.
entries.retirement: Not applicable while the schema addresses rows this way.

entries.purpose: Name a signed-in member's session, which is what the session cookie carries

strength.basis: Twenty-seven bytes drawn from SecureRandom, the width the session table stores.

entries.storageBoundary: Generated in the instance and stored in the session row the database keeps; the identifier travels in the host-bound session cookie. It reaches no log, export or screen: the member's own session list shows a truncated digest of it instead.
entries.permittedUse: Identifying a session. It is a bearer credential: whoever holds it is signed in, which is why the cookie is HttpOnly, Secure and host-bound and why every credential change ends the sessions of that account.
entries.rotation: Replaced at each moment trust is re-established. A sign-in and a successful password proof each store a new session, and the identifier presented before it stops resolving.
entries.revocation: Signing out, a credential change, a deactivation and the session-limit displacement each end sessions server-side, so a revoked identifier stops working rather than merely expiring.
entries.recovery: None is needed: an ended session is replaced by signing in again.
entries.retirement: A successor scheme takes effect for sessions created after it; sessions already stored keep the identifier they were issued.

entries.purpose: Prove that a state-changing request came from this application's own pages

strength.basis: Spring Security's cookie repository issues a version-4 UUID, 122 random bits. This project chooses neither the format nor the source, so it records what the framework produces instead of a number of its own.

entries.storageBoundary: Spring Security generates the value and places it in a cookie the frontend reads and echoes in a header. Nothing is stored server-side and this project does not generate the value.
entries.permittedUse: Comparing a request's header against its cookie. It is not an authenticator: it says the request came from this origin, never who made it.
entries.rotation: A new token is issued with the session it belongs to.
entries.revocation: Ending the session ends the token with it.
entries.recovery: None is needed.
entries.retirement: Follows Spring Security.

entries.purpose: Count failed sign-ins per client address, and instance-wide, without keeping the address in the counter

strength.basis: The collision resistance of SHA-256's 256-bit output. The digest keeps a username out of the table that counts failed sign-ins; it is not offered as protection against somebody who already guesses the username.

entries.storageBoundary: The instance database, as login_attempt_limit.subject_hash, where it is part of the primary key. It is written on every counted attempt and removed by the retention sweep that clears expired windows.
entries.permittedUse: Grouping attempts by address and instance-wide. The digest is not an authenticator, and it is not a pseudonym that may be published: the space of client addresses is small enough to search exhaustively, so a stored digest is a stored address with an extra step.
entries.rotation: Not applicable: no key exists. Rows age out with their window rather than being rotated.
entries.revocation: Not applicable.
entries.recovery: None is needed; the counters rebuild themselves from subsequent attempts.
entries.retirement: A successor digest changes what the stored subjects mean, so the existing rows are cleared with the change rather than migrated. Nothing outside the limiter reads them.

entries.purpose: Ask the breached-password service about a password without sending the password or its complete digest

parameters.protocol: Have I Been Pwned range API

strength.basis: The range protocol defines SHA-1, and the first five hex characters are all that leaves the instance. Nothing here rests on the digest's collision or preimage resistance, so the signature and integrity minimums do not reach it.

entries.storageBoundary: The complete digest exists only in application memory. Five hexadecimal characters are sent to the range service, and successful suffix ranges may remain in the bounded in-memory cache.
entries.permittedUse: The Have I Been Pwned range protocol only. SHA-1 carries no collision-resistance or credential-protection claim here, and neither the complete digest nor the password may leave the instance.
entries.rotation: The range service defines the protocol digest. A successor requires a protocol that preserves or improves the disclosure boundary before this use can change.
entries.revocation: Cached ranges expire by age and process restart; no key exists to revoke.
entries.recovery: None is needed; the digest is recomputed for each password check.
entries.retirement: Remove the client and its cache when the range protocol is replaced or retired.

entries.purpose: Let an account select one stored session for revocation without exposing its bearer session identifier

strength.basis: The second-preimage resistance of a 128-bit truncation of SHA-256, over a session identifier that itself carries 216 random bits, so there is no dictionary to invert. The truncation leaves only 64 bits against a collision, and that is not the property this use depends on: the handle selects one of an account's own sessions, and its input is a value the caller never chooses.

entries.storageBoundary: Computed from the high-entropy session identifier in application memory and returned by the authenticated account-session API. The handle is not stored separately.
entries.permittedUse: Resolving a revocation request among sessions already owned by the authenticated account. It never authenticates a caller and cannot address another account's sessions.
entries.rotation: Not applicable: no key exists, and each platform-generated session identifier produces its own handle.
entries.revocation: The handle stops resolving when its session ends or expires.
entries.recovery: None is needed; it is recomputed from active session identifiers.
entries.retirement: A successor digest may replace it without migrating stored state because handles are computed on read.

entries.purpose: Recognise a repeated booking request so a retry does not create a second booking

strength.basis: The collision resistance of SHA-256's 256-bit output. The fingerprint recognises a repeated request and protects nothing.

entries.storageBoundary: The instance database, beside the booking it identifies.
entries.permittedUse: Comparing one request to another, and only within the bookings of the member who sent it. It carries no security claim and protects nothing.
entries.rotation: Not applicable: no key.
entries.revocation: Not applicable.
entries.recovery: None is needed; it is recomputed from what it names.
entries.retirement: Replaceable with any digest, since nothing outside the instance reads it.

entries.purpose: Name the stored club logo so a browser can be told whether its copy is current

strength.basis: The collision resistance of SHA-256's 256-bit output. The digest is an ETag, so a collision would serve a stale image and nothing more.

entries.storageBoundary: The instance database, and the ETag it becomes.
entries.permittedUse: Cache validation. It is not an integrity guarantee against a party that can write the row.
entries.rotation: Not applicable: no key.
entries.revocation: Not applicable.
entries.recovery: None is needed; it is recomputed from what it names.
entries.retirement: Replaceable with any digest; a changed algorithm invalidates caches once.

entries.purpose: Name the rendering of the installed app's icons so a browser may keep one until the logo or the drawing changes

strength.basis: The collision resistance of SHA-256's 256-bit output over the logo digest and the rendering version. A collision would keep a stale icon cached and nothing more.

entries.storageBoundary: Computed per request and carried in the icon URLs of the manifest; nothing stores it.
entries.permittedUse: Cache validation of the served icons. It is not an integrity guarantee.
entries.rotation: Not applicable: no key.
entries.revocation: Not applicable.
entries.recovery: None is needed; it is recomputed from what it names.
entries.retirement: Replaceable with any digest; a changed algorithm invalidates cached icons once.

entries.purpose: Match an imported row against a person already on the roster

strength.basis: The collision resistance of SHA-256's 256-bit output, over the fields an import compares.

entries.storageBoundary: The instance database, on the imported reference.
entries.permittedUse: Deduplicating an import. It is not a pseudonym that may be published: it is taken over a name, an address and a membership type, whose space is small enough to search.
entries.rotation: Not applicable: no key.
entries.revocation: Not applicable.
entries.recovery: None is needed; it is recomputed from what it names.
entries.retirement: A change re-matches every stored reference, so it is made with an import run rather than in place.

entries.purpose: Name the seeded assessment dataset so a report says which data it was produced against

strength.basis: The collision resistance of SHA-256's 256-bit output, which names the dataset a run read.

entries.storageBoundary: Computed at runtime from a constant in the image; nothing is stored.
entries.permittedUse: Identifying a dataset in a report.
entries.rotation: Not applicable: no key.
entries.revocation: Not applicable.
entries.recovery: None is needed; it is recomputed from what it names.
entries.retirement: Replaceable with any digest.

entries.purpose: Name the serialized session attribute bytes decoded by the native assessment helper so its semantic projection can be compared with the disposable database observation

strength.basis: The collision resistance of SHA-256's 256-bit output. This digest names content and authenticates neither the database observation nor the projection.

entries.storageBoundary: Computed in memory by the separately packaged assessment fixture and returned with its semantic projection through stdout. Serialized bytes are supplied through stdin and are not returned. The observation belongs to private assessment evidence, not public reports.
entries.permittedUse: Comparing the exact serialized bytes with the bytes named by a projection. It is not a MAC, a credential, a tamper-proof receipt or an integrity guarantee against a party who can replace the observation and its digest.
entries.rotation: Not applicable: no key exists. Each observation computes its own digest.
entries.revocation: Not applicable.
entries.recovery: Repeat the observation and recompute the projection; no key or stored digest needs recovery.
entries.retirement: Introduce a successor digest with a new decoder contract before comparing observations produced under it.

entries.purpose: Name the native JDBC publication repository class bytes loaded by the separately packaged assessment helper alongside its fixed repository policy projection

strength.basis: The collision resistance of SHA-256's 256-bit output. This digest names class content and does not authenticate an image, a producer or an assessment result.

entries.storageBoundary: Computed in memory from one fixed native class resource in the assessment fixture and returned through stdout with the publication policy. The value belongs to private assessment binding evidence; no credentials or serialized session bytes are read by this projection.
entries.permittedUse: Comparing the loaded class content within an immutable candidate and fixture binding. It is not a MAC, a signature, a credential or independent proof that a replaceable class or observation is trustworthy.
entries.rotation: Not applicable: no key exists. Each projection computes the class digest again.
entries.revocation: Not applicable.
entries.recovery: Repeat the native projection against the recorded immutable candidate; no key needs recovery.
entries.retirement: Introduce a successor digest with a new projection contract before comparing observations produced under it.

entries.purpose: Give a submitted booking a client-side identity so a retry is recognised

strength.basis: Sixteen bytes drawn from the browser's Web Crypto. The key has to be unique across every client at once, because a repeat would suppress a booking somebody meant to make.

entries.storageBoundary: The browser, for the life of one submission.
entries.permittedUse: Identifying a request. It authenticates nothing, which is why the non-secure-context fallback is acceptable.
entries.rotation: Not applicable: every submission generates one.
entries.revocation: Not applicable.
entries.recovery: None is needed.
entries.retirement: Replaceable without a migration.

entries.purpose: Name an artefact, a configuration or a report the verification harness produced, so two runs can be compared

strength.basis: The collision resistance of SHA-256's 256-bit output, over the artefacts a verification run compares.

entries.storageBoundary: Build output and workflow artefacts. Nothing reaches an instance.
entries.permittedUse: Comparing and naming artefacts. No harness digest is a security control, and none may be presented as evidence that content was not tampered with by a party who could write it.
entries.rotation: Not applicable: no key.
entries.revocation: Not applicable.
entries.recovery: None is needed; a rerun recomputes everything.
entries.retirement: Replaceable with any digest.

entries.purpose: Give a verification run values nothing else uses, such as a scratch database name, a throwaway password or a correlation id

strength.basis: The smallest draw is four bytes for a run identifier, which only has to be unique inside one run. That minimum covers names, not secrets: where the harness draws a credential of its own it draws at least sixteen bytes, and a separate rule holds it there.

entries.storageBoundary: The lifetime of one verification run. Nothing is written to a tracked file and nothing reaches an instance.
entries.permittedUse: Test fixtures and correlation only. No harness value ever becomes an operational credential.
entries.rotation: Not applicable: every run generates its own.
entries.revocation: Not applicable.
entries.recovery: None is needed.
entries.retirement: Replaceable without a migration.

entries.purpose: Generate the database, bootstrap administrator, mail and identity credentials for a local club installation

strength.basis: Twenty-four bytes drawn by openssl rand, so each generated installation credential carries 192 bits of entropy.

entries.storageBoundary: Owner-only files below the installation's config and secrets directories. The bootstrap administrator credential is kept separately until the operator finalizes bootstrap; no generated credential is printed or written into a release directory.
entries.permittedUse: Authenticating the services of one local club installation and the first administrator sign-in. A generated value is never reused across installations.
entries.rotation: Reconfiguration retains existing credentials unless the operator deliberately replaces them. The bootstrap credential is replaced through the application and then removed with finalize-bootstrap.
entries.revocation: Replace the affected service credential and restart its consumers; finalize-bootstrap removes the initial administrator credential after it has been replaced.
entries.recovery: Restore the owner-only configuration and secret backup. If no backup exists, replace the affected credential through that service's recovery procedure rather than attempting to derive it.
entries.retirement: Remove the credential with the installation after any retained data has been migrated or destroyed.

entries.purpose: Generate the throwaway certificates and key pairs a verification run needs to exercise a TLS path

strength.basis: RSA-3072, the smallest modulus NIST rates at 128 bits. Each certificate lives for one run.

entries.storageBoundary: A temporary directory for the life of one run, or the ignored owner-only build/perf-mail for the life of one performance stack, and never a tracked file. Every certificate is self-signed and issued to a name under a reserved example domain, for a day except the performance relay's, which is issued for thirty because that stack is left standing between runs.
entries.permittedUse: Standing up a relay or a proxy a test then connects to. No generated key is ever trusted by an instance, published, or reused across runs.
entries.rotation: Each run generates its own; the performance stack reissues on every start and perf-reset removes the directory, so nothing outlives the stack that made it.
entries.revocation: Not applicable: no party trusts these beyond the run that made them.
entries.recovery: None is needed; a rerun generates new material.
entries.retirement: Replaced by whatever the tested transport requires.

entries.purpose: Let one pull request's installed upgrade gate serve its unpushed image under the official ghcr.io name from a loopback registry

strength.basis: RSA-3072, the smallest modulus NIST rates at 128 bits. The certificate authority and the registry certificate are issued for one day.

entries.storageBoundary: The ignored build/installed-upgrade-gate/certificates directory for the life of one gate run. The authority's key is deleted as soon as it has signed the registry certificate, and the directory is removed before the run's evidence is uploaded.
entries.permittedUse: Making the runner's Docker daemon trust a registry on 127.0.0.1:443 that answers for ghcr.io during that one run. Nothing else trusts the authority, and the trust and hosts entries are withdrawn when the run ends.
entries.rotation: Each run issues its own authority and certificate.
entries.revocation: Not applicable: the trust entry is removed with the run, and nothing else trusts the authority.
entries.recovery: None is needed; a rerun issues new material.
entries.retirement: Replaced if a pull request's image can be served without impersonating the official registry name.

entries.purpose: Generate the private identity for real STARTTLS mail and HTTPS password-breach forwarding inside one disposable security environment

strength.basis: The generated RSA modulus is 3072 bits, rated at 128 bits of security. This describes the fixture key, not the cipher suite negotiated by the TLS implementations.

entries.storageBoundary: The ignored per-run mail directory below build/security includes the full random instance fingerprint in its name. It is created with mode 0700 and its unencrypted key.pem has mode 0600. Mailpit and the bounded password-breach bridge read the certificate and private key through read-only bind mounts. Retained private diagnostic assets can outlive teardown; no key, certificate fingerprint or raw mail is published or tracked.
entries.permittedUse: Presenting the self-signed certificate for the exact DNS names mail and password-breach in the disposable SECURITY environment. The application and seeder trust it through the separate fixture truststore entry. X509Certificate checks both hostnames and the self-signature; fingerprint256 records private metadata and does not perform TLS peer pinning.
entries.rotation: The first start attempt creates a fresh certificate unconditionally. Bind retries within that same start retain the same identity and assets. A new random instance uses a distinct directory even when the run ID is reused, and never reuses retained material.
entries.revocation: Remove the run-owned consumers and their trust configuration to stop using the identity. There is no external authority or revocation service. Retaining a diagnostic key does not extend trust into a new instance.
entries.recovery: Retained material is diagnostic evidence, not a backup for a fresh environment. Start a new instance to create a new key and certificate; existing same-start retry assets are not regenerated or independently revalidated by the retry path.
entries.retirement: Stop all consumers before replacing the fixture identity scheme. Retained private diagnostic assets remain under the operator's evidence-retention control rather than being silently deleted by teardown.

entries.purpose: Preserve candidate CA anchors and add private dependency trust for STARTTLS and bounded HTTPS forwarding without disabling issuer or hostname validation

strength.basis: The added OpenSSL-generated RSA-3072 fixture anchor has 128 bits of security. This rates that anchor, not the candidate default CA policy, TLS cipher suite or PKCS12 protection algorithms. The candidate JDK implements truststore conversion, certificate import, validation and TLS negotiation; no suite or store protection algorithm is selected here.

entries.storageBoundary: The digest-bound candidate image keytool first imports its existing default CA anchors into per-instance mail.p12, then adds cert.pem as a trusted certificate without a private-key entry. An offline bounded container runs as the host numeric owner. The owner-only parent directory protects retained assets; mode 0444 allows non-root application and seeder users to read their read-only mounts. The fixed store password is not a credential or confidentiality boundary.
entries.permittedUse: Setting javax.net.ssl.trustStore for the application and seeder JVMs in the disposable SECURITY environment. The separate process-wide store preserves their candidate default CA anchors and adds the local mail/password-breach identity. STARTTLS and hostname validation remain required. The bridge verifies the official upstream with the pinned Caddy image default CA policy. Fixture fingerprints remain metadata rather than peer pins. Never install this fixture anchor in a club deployment.
entries.rotation: Import the newly generated certificate for each new instance before starting its consumers. Same-start bind retries reuse that instance's truststore. Replacing a truststore requires restarting its JVM consumers; retained stores are not reused by a fresh instance.
entries.revocation: Stop the run-owned JVM consumers and withdraw their truststore configuration. No certificate revocation service is configured for this isolated fixture authority.
entries.recovery: A failed initial import stops startup rather than enabling unverified TLS. Create a new instance and import its fresh certificate instead of reusing retained diagnostic assets from an older instance.
entries.retirement: Remove the JVM truststore configuration and mounts with the fixture relay scheme. Retained public-certificate stores and private keys stay within the private diagnostic evidence boundary until the operator retires those assets.

entries.purpose: Recognise one expected certificate by its digest instead of trusting whoever a certificate authority vouched for

strength.basis: The collision resistance of SHA-256's 256-bit output. A second certificate carrying the same digest is what the pin would have to be fooled by, and that is the property SHA-256 supplies.

entries.storageBoundary: The expected value is held outside the code that checks it: a launch argument for a browser, an environment value for the mail peer. No digest of a production certificate is tracked in this repository.
entries.permittedUse: Deciding whether the party at the other end is the expected one. Unlike the content hashes above, this is a security control: a mismatch refuses the connection rather than being reported.
entries.rotation: Replacing the pinned certificate means replacing the expectation in the same change; the two are held apart on purpose, so changing only one fails closed.
entries.revocation: Removing the expectation stops the pinned path rather than falling back to an unpinned one.
entries.recovery: A pin that no longer matches is a refusal, not a loss: the expectation is corrected and the run repeated.
entries.retirement: A successor digest is introduced by pinning under it before the previous expectation is removed.

entries.purpose: Let anybody verify that a published image was published by this repository's release workflow

strength.basis: Sigstore issues the ephemeral key and chooses the signature hash. The workflow pins cosign by digest and verifies the signature it produced rather than selecting its parameters.

entries.storageBoundary: No long-lived private key exists. Sigstore issues a short-lived certificate against the workflow's OIDC identity and records the signature in a public transparency log.
entries.permittedUse: Signing a published image. It says which workflow published the image, not that the image is free of defects; the release workflow signs the digest the release candidate workflow built and qualified.
entries.rotation: Every signing operation obtains a new short-lived certificate; there is nothing to rotate on a schedule.
entries.revocation: Not applicable to a keyless signature. A withdrawn release is deleted and stated as withdrawn.
entries.recovery: None is possible or needed: no material can be lost, and a signature is produced again by re-running the release.
entries.retirement: Replaced by changing the signing action, which changes what a verifier is told to expect.

entries.purpose: Let acceptance users verify that a nightly image passed this repository's nightly image workflow before its public tags moved

strength.basis: Sigstore issues the ephemeral key and chooses the signature hash. The workflow pins cosign and every attestation action, binds the selected verified commit in a signed source predicate, and verifies their workflow identity before it publishes a nightly tag.

entries.storageBoundary: No long-lived private key exists. The public registry holds the signature, provenance, selected-source and SBOM attestations beside the qualified image digest.
entries.permittedUse: Signing and attesting a qualified acceptance image. The identity is distinct from a release signature and grants no release status.
entries.rotation: Every nightly publication obtains a new short-lived certificate; there is nothing to rotate on a schedule.
entries.revocation: Not applicable to a keyless signature. Retention removes an obsolete nightly image and its attached manifests only after no retained tag reaches them.
entries.recovery: None is possible or needed: no signing material can be lost, and the next verified revision produces new evidence.
entries.retirement: Replaced by changing the nightly signing workflow and the verification identity documented with it.

entries.purpose: Publish where an image came from and what it contains, signed by the workflow that published it

strength.basis: The same keyless identity signs the attestation, so Sigstore chooses the key and the hash. The workflow pins the attestation actions by digest and verifies what they published.

entries.storageBoundary: Same keyless identity as the release signature; the attestation is pushed to the registry beside the image.
entries.permittedUse: Attesting build provenance and the software bill of materials. The provenance names the release run that published the digest; the build ran in the release candidate run the release evidence names. It records what a run did, not that the result is correct.
entries.rotation: Each run attests under its own short-lived certificate.
entries.revocation: Not applicable to a keyless attestation.
entries.recovery: None is possible or needed.
entries.retirement: Replaced by changing the attesting action.

entries.purpose: Encrypt and authenticate what a member's browser sends to the instance

strength.basis: The proxy obtains the certificate itself for a club's own domain and negotiates the suite with each browser, so this repository selects neither the key nor the cipher. What a running instance actually offers is read by the passive assessment rather than claimed here.

entries.storageBoundary: The reverse proxy's own storage. For a club's own domain the proxy obtains the certificate itself and Courtside never sees the key. The verification profiles are different and say so: they run the proxy with an internal certificate authority, so a local root and its leaf keys exist inside those containers for the life of a run.
entries.permittedUse: The public entry point. Courtside ships no production certificate authority, generates no production key material and states no cipher list of its own. The internal authority is for the verification profiles and must not be used to serve a club.
entries.rotation: The proxy obtains and renews certificates itself; an operator supplying their own owns the renewal.
entries.revocation: The issuing authority's, and the operator's to request.
entries.recovery: A lost certificate is reissued by the authority; nothing in Courtside needs to be recovered with it.
entries.retirement: Follows what the proxy supports.

entries.purpose: Encrypt and authenticate the connection an instance hands its outgoing messages to

strength.basis: The relay and the receiving server negotiate the suite, and the relay's certificate is the operator's. This repository decides only that the connection must use STARTTLS; whether the relay's certificate is checked is an operator switch that defaults to checking it.

entries.storageBoundary: The relay's certificate, read by the instance. In the reference deployment the proxy's certificate pair for the mail hostname is copied into a volume the mail container reads, so that deployment does hold a private key on the operator's own host; nothing is copied out of it and no key is tracked in this repository.
entries.permittedUse: Reaching the relay over an encrypted connection. STARTTLS is required rather than opportunistic, so a relay that cannot negotiate it is refused instead of being spoken to in the clear. Trusting an unverified relay certificate is a deliberate, separately named setting.
entries.rotation: The relay's own renewal, which the instance observes rather than performs; a certificate whose remaining life falls below the configured share is reported.
entries.revocation: The issuing authority's.
entries.recovery: A relay that cannot present a usable certificate refuses the connection, and the message is retried four times over about a minute. After that the message is recorded as failed, and failed is terminal: nothing redelivers it later, so a relay outage longer than that ladder loses the send and the message log is where an operator sees it.
entries.retirement: Follows the relay.

entries.purpose: Sign outgoing mail so a receiving server can tell it came from the club's domain

strength.basis: Stalwart generates the keys and chooses the RSA modulus; its automatic management exposes no key-size setting. What the reference deployment does decide is the algorithm set, and it enables Dkim1Ed25519Sha256 and Dkim1RsaSha256 with no SHA-1 variant.

entries.storageBoundary: The mail container's volume in the reference deployment, where the container generates the key itself. The public half is a DNS record the operator publishes. No key is tracked in this repository.
entries.permittedUse: Signing the club's own outgoing mail.
entries.rotation: The operator publishes a new selector, signs under it, and retires the old record once nothing in flight relies on it.
entries.revocation: Removing the DNS record for a selector.
entries.recovery: A lost key is replaced by generating a new one under a new selector; no past message needs to be recoverable.
entries.retirement: The selector's DNS record is withdrawn after the change has propagated.

entries.purpose: Carry the instance's database traffic, which includes session rows, password hashes and the hashed login subjects
entries.algorithm: TLS, when an operator requires it; the driver's own opportunistic default otherwise

strength.basis: The driver and the server negotiate the suite, and the authority an operator configures is theirs. This repository decides only which mode an instance runs in.

entries.storageBoundary: The connection between the application container and the database container, and the operator's own authority file where one is configured. Courtside reads that file and holds no material of its own; the reference deployment ships no certificate and defaults to the driver's opportunistic mode, which encrypts when the database offers it and verifies nothing.
entries.permittedUse: Reaching the database. `courtside.database.tls.mode` decides what that means: `prefer` leaves the driver alone, `disable` refuses encryption, and `verify-full` requires a certificate that chains to the configured authority and names the host the connection URL names. Verified mode refuses to start when the authority is missing or unreadable, when the connection URL or the pool carries something that would decide the transport instead, and when no connection pool was configured with it at all.
entries.rotation: The operator's, on their own authority and server certificate. Courtside reads the authority file for every new connection, so a replaced file takes effect without a restart and a replaced one that no longer vouches for the database refuses the next connection rather than falling back.
entries.revocation: The issuing authority's. Courtside performs no revocation check of its own.
entries.recovery: An authority file that no longer matches is a refusal, not a loss: the operator restores the right file, or sets the mode back to `prefer`.
entries.retirement: Encrypting the reverse proxy's connection to the application is the remaining half of this path and has its own entry.

entries.purpose: Separate one signed-in account's offline booking cache from every account or session state that follows it

strength.basis: The 122 random bits a version-4 UUID draws. The value is a uniqueness marker rather than a secret: no authorisation depends on guessing it, and a mismatch always rejects the cached response.

entries.storageBoundary: The member's browser stores the current value in a dedicated Cache Storage control entry and copies it into the personal-booking cache response. It names no person and leaves neither browser nor device.
entries.permittedUse: Correlating a cached personal-booking response with the account generation that created it. It authenticates nobody and grants no server access.
entries.rotation: Every successful login, logout, session refusal and personal-cache invalidation replaces the marker before the old response is deleted.
entries.revocation: Writing the next marker immediately makes every response carrying the prior value unusable, even if deleting that response is delayed.
entries.recovery: None is needed: a missing or unreadable marker rejects offline authority, and the next online personal-booking read creates another one.
entries.retirement: A successor invalidation scheme clears both browser caches before it accepts personal data under its own marker.

entries.purpose: Carry what the reverse proxy forwards to the application, which includes the session cookie and a password on its way in
entries.algorithm: TLS, when an operator turns it on; plain HTTP on the compose network otherwise

strength.basis: The proxy and the application negotiate the suite over the operator's own certificate pair. This repository decides only whether the hop is encrypted at all.

entries.storageBoundary: The connection between the proxy container and the application container, and the operator's own certificate, key and authority files where they are configured. Courtside reads them and holds no material of its own; the reference deployment ships none and defaults to plain HTTP on a network private to the compose project.
entries.permittedUse: Reaching the application from the proxy. `courtside.server.tls.mode` decides what that means: `plaintext` leaves the hop as HTTP, and `serve` makes the application serve the operator's certificate while the proxy trusts nothing but the authority the operator names. One setting drives both ends. Serving mode refuses to start when the certificate or the key is missing, unreadable, holds what the other one should, has expired or is not valid yet, or is protected by a password this instance is given no way to open, and when Spring's own `server.ssl` configuration would decide what is served instead.
entries.rotation: The operator's, on their own authority, certificate and key. Both services read their file once at start, so a replacement takes effect when the service that reads it restarts.
entries.revocation: The issuing authority's. Courtside performs no revocation check of its own.
entries.recovery: Material that no longer matches is a refusal, not a loss: the application refuses to start, the proxy refuses the hop with a bad gateway rather than falling back to plain text, and the operator restores the right file or sets the mode back to `plaintext`.
entries.retirement: What would be retired here is the plaintext default, and only a deployment that already runs an authority can retire it. Courtside issues no material, so it cannot make the encrypted hop the default for a club that has none.
